commonMistakes: Rounding the lower back to reach further down
Bending the knees into a squat instead of hinging at the hips
Letting the weight drift away from the legs
cues: Push your hips straight back, like closing a car door behind you
Weight slides down your thighs, close to your body
Feel a deep stretch in the hamstrings, then squeeze the glutes to stand
instructions: Stand tall holding the weight in front of your thighs, feet hip-width apart, knees softly bent.
Brace your core and push your hips straight back, letting the weight slide down the fronts of your thighs.
Keep your back flat and your chest proud as you lower until you feel a deep stretch in your hamstrings, usually just below the knees.
Drive your hips forward and squeeze your glutes to return to standing. Do not hyperextend your lower back at the top.
longevityNotes: The hip hinge is the movement you use every time you pick something off the floor — groceries, grandchildren, a dropped pen. Training it keeps the posterior chain (glutes, hamstrings, spinal erectors) strong and teaches a spine-safe lifting pattern that protects your back for decades. Load it progressively but never maximally; a crisp, controlled hinge at RPE 7 beats a sloppy max that costs you a disc.
name: Romanian Deadlift

progression.loadingGuidance: Add 2-5 kg when you can complete 3 sets of 10 with a flat back and full hamstring stretch at RPE 7 or less.
progression.progressTo: Barbell Romanian deadlift from a deficit
progression.regressTo: Dowel hip-hinge drill (no weight, dowel along the spine)

safetyNotes: If you have an acute disc issue or radiating leg pain, skip loaded hinging until cleared by your clinician. Stop the set the moment your lower back starts to round — depth is earned, not forced.
